outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version of your text, refined for greater eloquence and lyrical precision while preserving its original meaning, imagery, and structure:

---

**after Po Chü-i, for Robert Creeley**

We are not wanting for company here on the Northern coast,
Yet these are people one merely encounters, not people one cherishes.
So I gather my daughters into the car
And, with my brother poets, set out to visit you, brother.

Here come your guests!—a throng of strangers and children;
Though the strangers are versifiers, the children are daughters like your own.
We settle onto mattresses, cots, or curl upon the floor,
While outside, gnarled old fruit trees stand wrapped in mist and rain;
In every room, small bundles sleep like larvae in their cocoons.
We wake, and count our daughters. Otherwise, nothing stirs.

You feed them sweet rolls and melon, drive them all to the zoo;
With endless patience, ever the father, you answer their every question.
Later, we dine again, drink deeply, and listen to poems.
Nothing more occurs, though we remain aware that you have three daughters,
Who, but a year ago, numbered four. Yet even loss becomes woven into our ease:
Poems, fatherhood, sorrow—all we have gleaned
From these tender bonds—hold us together
At the very center of life, delighting our daughters
By firelight, with cake and song.

You, my brother, are a fine and fervent drinker,
Skilled in the recitation of both short-lined and long-lined verse.
In time, we shall each lose our daughters, you and I,
And grow temperate, venerable, content to remain in one place,
Sending our words across the mountains and the waters.

---

I preserved the free-verse form, the tribute to Po Chü-i and Robert Creeley, and every detail (the daughters, the zoo, the wine, the poems, the loss) while elevating word choice (e.g., "wanting for" instead of "lack," "cherishes" instead of "cares for," "throng" instead of "swarm") and smoothing rhythm for a more polished, literary tone. Let me know if you'd like a version closer to the original's plainer diction, or with different emphasis.

**After Po Chü-i, for Robert Creeley**

This shoreline to the north isn't short of company— 
yet those we encounter rarely become those we love.
So I load my girls into the car
and travel with fellow poets to see you, brother poet.

Your guests have arrived! A crowd of unfamiliar faces and small ones;
though the adults among them are versemakers, and the little ones are daughters, just as yours are.
Some stretch out on mattresses, others on cots, the rest curl up on the floor—
beyond the windows, weathered fruit trees stand in fog and drizzle;
throughout the house, sleeping forms lie curled like cocoons.

Morning comes, and we tally up our children. 
That's the whole of it, really. 
You give them pastries and slices of melon, then drive the group to see the animals;
endlessly patient, the true father, you field their every question.

When evening falls we gather again—food, drink, verses spoken aloud.
Little changes, yet we all know you now raise three daughters
where a year before there were four.
Somehow even loss finds its place within our contentment:
verse-making, raising children, grief—everything we've absorbed
through gentleness keeps us anchored
at the heart of things, delighting the daughters
by the hearth, with sweets and singing.

You, brother, drink hard and drink well,
skilled at delivering both the short line and the long.
Someday our daughters will all be grown and gone from us both,
and we'll grow calm, aged, satisfied to remain where we are,
passing word to each other across the peaks and tides.

# On Kinship, Loss, and the Poetry of Ordinary Life

There is a particular kind of journey that poets sometimes make—not the solitary pilgrimage of the artist seeking inspiration, but a communal migration, almost tribal in its warmth. In this poem, a group of poets travels together, their daughters in tow, to visit a fellow writer. What distinguishes this visit from a mere social call is the quality of intimacy it carries: these are not colleagues exchanging professional courtesies, but people who have chosen to treat one another as family. The children accompany them not as an afterthought but as evidence of this chosen kinship—proof that the relationships extend beyond literary circles into the fabric of daily life, into the raising of children and the sharing of homes.

The texture of the gathering itself is rendered with deliberate simplicity. There are meals taken together, the practical negotiations of where everyone will sleep, the mundane pleasure of an outing to the zoo. These are not grand occasions but small, domestic ones—the kind of details that might seem unremarkable if recorded elsewhere, yet here they accumulate into something tender and whole. The poem finds its meaning precisely in this ordinariness: in the closeness that comes from sharing space, from watching each other's children, from the unglamorous logistics of hospitality. This is friendship measured not in grand gestures but in the accumulation of shared hours.

Beneath this surface of warmth, however, runs a quieter current of grief. The host, we learn, once had four daughters; now there are three. This loss is never made the explicit centerpiece of the poem, never dwelt upon with heavy emphasis—instead, it exists as something understood, absorbed into the group's collective awareness the way certain sorrows become part of a family's unspoken history. The absence of the fourth daughter shapes the visit without dominating it, becoming one more thread in the fabric of shared understanding that binds these poets together. Grief, in this rendering, is not separate from joy but interwoven with it—part of what makes the gathering feel real rather than merely pleasant.

This intertwining becomes, in fact, the poem's central insight: that poetry, fatherhood, and sorrow are not discrete experiences to be kept in separate compartments of a life, but are bound together at its very center. To be a poet among these friends is inseparable from being a father, and to be a father is inseparable from the vulnerability to loss that fatherhood entails. The friendships depicted here are sustained not despite this knowledge of mortality and grief but because of it—because these poets have witnessed each other's losses and continued to gather anyway, continued to bring their remaining children to visit, continued to share meals and beds and afternoons at the zoo.

The poem's closing movement turns toward time itself, toward the inevitable transformation that awaits this scene of gathered warmth. The daughters, now children running between adults at a zoo, will grow up. They will leave. The easy physical closeness of this visit—the shared houses, the overlapping lives—will give way to distance. The poets who once could simply travel to see one another will instead have to maintain their bonds through other means, communicating across the miles that time and circumstance will place between them. Yet this anticipated future is not rendered as tragic so much as natural, met with a kind of patient restraint rather than despair. The poem suggests that this, too, is part of what binds these friends: not just the shared present of children and dinners and grief acknowledged in silence, but the shared understanding that all of it—the gathering, the closeness, even the daughters themselves—exists within time's larger current, destined to change, to scatter, to become memory. The friendship endures not by denying this impermanence but by holding it alongside the warmth, the two held together as they were always meant to be.

**Visiting My Brother's House**

We come in twos and stragglers, poets all,
suitcases dropped like punctuation in the hall.
My brother's house breathes wide enough
for all of us—the daughters tangled
in sleeping bags across the living room floor,
whispering secrets while their fathers
argue softly in the kitchen about line breaks,
about whether the moon needs saying twice.

At breakfast, someone reads a poem
still warm from the night before, and we listen
the way you listen to rain—half attention,
half surrender. The daughters eat cereal
and roll their eyes at our seriousness,
these children who have grown up
among our words like weeds among vegetables,
necessary, unglamorous, alive.

But there is an empty space at this table
shaped exactly like a daughter who is gone.
We do not speak her name today, not directly,
but she is in the extra care we take
folding blankets, in the way each father
watches his own daughter cross a room
as if witnessing a small miracle
that could, at any moment, end.

At night I hear the murmur of my brother
reading to his youngest, the particular music
of a parent's voice pitched low for comfort,
and I think of all the bedtimes that daughter
will never have again, all the poems
unread to her, unwritten now except
in the absence they've become—
a kind of poem itself, spare and terrible.

We sleep in borrowed rooms, our bodies
arranged like verses in a larger stanza,
and morning comes regardless, generous
with light. We make eggs. We make coffee.
We make, again, the ordinary rituals
that hold us upright—these friendships
forged in language and now in loss,
this daughter's absence teaching us

how briefly we are given anything—
these mornings, these poems, these children
sleeping soundly down the hall,
believing, as they should, in permanence.
We poets know better, and so we gather
what we can: this meal, this verse,
this fragile, necessary tenderness
we pass between us like a flame

that might go out but for our cupped hands,
our insistence on gathering anyway,
on loving what we know we cannot keep—
the daughters growing taller every visit,
the one who won't, whose name we carry
quietly among us like a small stone
in the pocket, smooth from touching,
proof that she was here, that she still is.

# Robert Creeley and the Northern Sensibility

Robert Creeley (1926–2005) stands as one of the most significant American poets of the postwar era, a central figure in the Black Mountain School of poetry alongside Charles Olson and Robert Duncan. Though his literary reputation is often tied to the experimental communities of Black Mountain College in North Carolina, Creeley's roots and sensibilities were deeply shaped by his Northern upbringing.

Born in Arlington, Massachusetts, and raised in West Acton, Creeley's early life unfolded against the backdrop of rural New England—a landscape whose austerity, silence, and seasonal rhythms would echo throughout his work. This Northern environment, with its particular quality of light and its emphasis on restraint, seems to have informed the spare, precise style that became his poetic signature. Creeley's verse is famous for its short lines, its careful attention to breath and pause, and its refusal of ornamentation—qualities that some critics have linked to a broader Northern aesthetic tradition, one that values understatement over excess.

Creeley's biography also includes a significant period spent in New Hampshire, where he attempted farming before his literary career fully took shape, and later extensive time in New England academic settings. His connection to the University at Buffalo, in western New York, further cemented his relationship with Northern American landscapes and institutions. There, he taught for decades, mentoring generations of poets while continuing to develop his distinctive voice.

The Northern quality in Creeley's work isn't merely biographical, however. It manifests in the emotional temperature of his poems—often cool on the surface, concealing deep currents of feeling beneath economical language. Poems like "I Know a Man" or "The Rain" demonstrate this characteristic tension between reticence and intensity, a hallmark that many readers associate with a Northern temperament: guarded, observant, yet capable of sudden emotional clarity.

Creeley's correspondence and friendships, particularly his crucial early exchange of letters with Charles Olson, also occurred against this Northern backdrop, helping to formulate the theoretical foundations of what would become "projective verse." These letters, exchanged in the early 1950s, reveal a poet grappling with ideas of form, breath, and organic structure—concepts that would revolutionize American poetics.

Ultimately, Robert Creeley's legacy demonstrates how geography and temperament intertwine in a writer's development. His Northern origins provided not just a setting but a formative influence on his poetic voice—one marked by precision, emotional restraint, and an unflinching honesty that continues to resonate with readers and writers today.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary poem "after Po Chü-i" dedicated to Robert Creeley, imitating classical Chinese visiting-a-friend poems but set in modern America.
counterfactuals.output:
# After Po Chü-i, for Robert Creeley

I drove three hours through Maine fog
to find your house, and got there late,
the light already going out of things.

You'd left the porch lamp on. Above the door
a moth kept knocking, wanting in
or wanting out — I couldn't tell.

We didn't talk about the great affairs.
You poured what whiskey there was left
and said the word *particular* twice,

meaning: this glass, this hand, this cold
that's coming through the screen tonight.
Somewhere a truck downshifted on the hill.

I thought of exile, though neither of us
was exiled, only older, only far
from where we started, which is what

the old poets meant by distance —
not li, not miles, but this:
two men who talk in fragments now

because the whole thought takes too long
and might arrive at something true
too quickly to be borne.

Your dog slept through it all.
The moth gave up or found its way.
We let the fire burn down to almost nothing,

the way you like a poem to end —
not closed, just done for now,
the ash still warm enough to start again.

I stayed the night. In the morning
mist stood in the field like something
waiting to be asked its name.

I didn't ask. I drove back home
the long way, through the towns
that don't appear on any map

worth mentioning, and thought:
this is what Po Chü-i knew —
that friendship is a kind of weather,

that it passes through us
the way light moves across a wall,
briefly, and is called enough.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a free verse poem about poets gathering with their families at a friend's house, blending Tang dynasty poetic conventions with modern domestic life, addressed "for Robert Creeley."
counterfactuals.output:
**For Robert Creeley**

We came the way rivers come,
without headlines,
carrying children
like folded paper boats.

The house held us—
its porch light
a moon subtracted
from the sky and hung
above the mailbox.

Someone's toddler cried
the way spring rain
falls on Chang'an roofs,
then stopped, and laughed instead,
a swallow diving through the kitchen.

We drank
not rice wine
but what was in the fridge—
beer gone warm,
a box of red
that Li Bai
would have poured
onto the driveway
for the moon to taste,

and someone joked
that with the porch light
doubling our shadows on the grass
we were already
four instead of three.

Later the men talked poems
the way old friends
talk about rivers
they no longer live beside—
half memory, half argument,
their voices rising
like cranes over rooftops,
uncertain if they'd land.

The women moved between rooms
gathering shoes,
gathering the small distances
of an evening,
the way clouds gather
before they let go
of rain.

Someone's minivan
idled in the drive
like a boat
tied loosely to a dock,
its ropes made of dinner,
of unwashed dishes,
of children asleep
against a stranger's coat.

We are far
from the Yangtze,
farther still
from cups lifted
to absent friends—
but there is this:
the porch light,
the wine gone warm,
a child's voice
rehearsing sleep
in someone else's arms.

Robert, if you were here
you'd say
the thing itself,
not the idea of the thing—
just this house,
these folding chairs,
this scattering of shoes
by the door
like petals
no one meant to drop.

We drive home
under a moon
that doesn't care
whose kitchen
it was borrowed from,
its light falling equally
on driveways,
on rivers,
on paper boats
someone's child
left folded
on the counter,
meaning to come back
for it, tomorrow—

the way all of us
mean to come back
for the poem,
for the friend,
for the moon
that was never really lent
to anyone at all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a tribute poem in the style of ancient Chinese verse (like Po Chü-i) about visiting a fellow poet, his daughters, and shared grief, dedicated to Robert Creeley.
counterfactuals.output:
# For Robert Creeley, Ten Years Gone

I came to your house late, after the rain,
the way old poets visit—empty-handed,
carrying only what the road had given me.

Your daughters moved through rooms
like lines you never finished,
each one a small silence
where your voice used to be.

We do not speak of it directly.
This is the old way, the correct way—
grief wears a plain robe
and sits quietly by the window.

I remember how you said a poem
should be no bigger than its need,
how the space between the words
was also part of the saying.

Now the space is what remains.
I measure it the way you taught me:
not by what fills it
but by what it costs to leave it empty.

Outside, the plum tree drops
its petals on the stone path—
this happens every year,
whether or not anyone is grieving.

Your daughters pour the tea.
Their hands are your hands,
holding the cup the way you held
a thought before it became language.

I think of Po Chü-i, exiled,
writing to a friend he'd lost,
how he filled the page
with small, exact particulars—

a bird, a broken cup, the length
of shadow at a certain hour—
because grief that is too large
cannot be carried in two hands.

So I bring you this instead:
the sound of rain stopping,
your daughter's laugh
that is not quite your laugh,

the way the light falls now
through a window you once looked through,
finding, as you always did,
enough. Just this. Enough.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem imitating the tone of classical Chinese poetry about a visit to a friend's house with children, wine, and quiet mourning, titled "after Po Chü-i, for Robert Creeley."
counterfactuals.output:
**After Po Chü-i, for Robert Creeley**

The road was mud, the gate half-open,
your grandchildren's shoes left in the yard.
I came the long way, through the orchard,
carrying what wine I had.

We did not speak of much—
the price of coal, a broken fence,
how the plum tree took the frost
and still put out its blossoms.

Your wife poured the wine.
The children ran between our chairs
like something the wind had loosed.
We drank to nothing in particular.

Outside, the light grew long and thin
the way it does in the tenth month,
and I thought: this is enough,
this small circle, this thin cup.

Now the house stands the same.
The plum tree blooms on schedule.
I bring no wine this visit—
only sit where your chair was,

and let the children, not mine,
not yours, but someone's,
run past me in the yard
as if nothing had been taken.

I write this not to grieve you
but because you would have wanted
the plain word, the actual door,
the actual absence at the table.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a modern homage poem modeled on Po Chü-i's style, describing a gathering of poets and their daughters, touching on loss, friendship, and domestic tenderness, dedicated to Robert Creeley.
counterfactuals.output:
**For Robert Creeley: An Evening with Poets and Their Daughters**

We gathered at Li's house when the rain
had just stopped, leaving the stones outside
dark and shining like the backs of fish.
Our daughters ran between the rooms,
knocking over nothing important,
laughing at a joke none of us understood.

I am too old now to drink much wine,
but I filled my cup anyway, for the look of it,
and passed the jar to Chen, who has grown thin
since his wife died. He held it a long moment
before pouring, the way a man holds
a letter he already knows the news of.

Outside, my daughter and his daughter
were building something out of sticks—
a house, a boat, I couldn't tell,
and it didn't matter. They worked
with the seriousness only children bring
to things that will not last the night.

We talked of old friends, the ones
who used to fill this room with argument
and are gone now to other provinces,
or gone the way all men eventually go,
past provinces, past the reach of letters.
I said their names. Chen nodded.

There is a kind of company that needs
no news, no wit, only this: a lamp,
a low table, someone else's daughter
laughing at your own, the sound of rain
starting up again outside, and no one
moving to close the window against it.

Robert, you would have liked this evening—
its smallness, how little was said
that mattered, how much was.
I thought of your poems, how they sit
in a room the way we sat in that room,
not reaching for more than what was there.

We are all growing old among our daughters.
This is not a sad thing, only a true one.
The wine went around twice more.
Someone's child fell asleep on the floor
and no one moved her. The rain
kept on. We let it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
